scenario: AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I would tell her whenever she used too little salt or too much spice, if something was a little burnt or undercooked, told her when I knew how to make the dish better next time etc. I would always eat all of it and say thank you so it was not like I was being rude about it. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

Here’s my assessment: ### **Was it wrong? (Answer: 1)** **Yes, you stepped over a line in this case.** Here’s why: 1. **Constructive Criticism vs. Humiliation** - Your intent was likely helpful, but the *delivery* and *context* were problematic. While you framed it as constructive criticism, your girlfriend perceived it as **passive-aggressive** (e.g., "if you’re so much better, you can do it yourself") and **undermining** (especially when your mom was involved). - Even if you ate everything and thanked her, the **pattern of criticism** (even if well-intentioned) can feel like **micromanagement** or **control**, especially in a relationship where she’s already taking on a role (cooking) she may not fully enjoy or feel confident in. 2. **The Mom Factor** - Inviting your mom to "help" your girlfriend was a **huge misstep**. It framed her cooking as **deficient in front of family**, which is a **huge emotional trigger** for many people. Even if your mom was kind, the **suggestion itself** made her feel exposed and judged. - This is why she "snapped" afterward—she felt **shamed** in a way that went beyond the usual cooking critiques. 3. **Power Dynamics & Role Expectations** - You agreed she’d cook because she got home earlier, but **she may not actually want to cook**. If she’s resentful about it (even if she hasn’t said so), your critiques could feel like **gaslighting** ("You’re not doing it right, but you *have* to do it"). - If she’s **not enjoying cooking**, forcing her (even indirectly) to improve could make her feel **trapped** in a role she didn’t choose. 4. **The "Cooking Strike" as a Boundary** - Her refusal to cook is **not overreacting**—it’s a **healthy boundary**. If she feels **humiliated, controlled, or resentful**, withdrawing a labor of love (cooking) is a **valid protest**. This isn’t just about food; it’s about **respect and emotional safety**. --- ### **What You Could Do Now** Since you care about her and the relationship, here’s how to **repair this**: 1. **Apologize Specifically (Not Just "I’m Sorry")** - Instead of just saying you’re sorry for the mom comment, **acknowledge how it made her feel**: *"I realize now that suggesting my mom help you cook made you feel exposed and judged, even if that wasn’t my intention. I should’ve known that would hurt you."* - **Don’t defend your critiques**—just own that you **didn’t consider her feelings enough**. 2. **Stop the Cooking Critiques (For Now)** - If you want to help, **ask how** she’d like feedback. Maybe she’d prefer: - A **shared cooking session** (you both learn together). - **Specific praise** for things she does well. - **No critiques at all**—just enjoying her efforts. 3. **Revisit the Cooking Agreement** - Ask her **honestly** how she feels about cooking. Is it a chore? Does she enjoy it? Maybe you can **take turns** or find a compromise (e.g., she cooks 3x/week, you handle the rest). 4. **Focus on Rebuilding Trust** - Small gestures (e.g., helping with a chore she hates, or just listening to her frustrations) can **show you’re on her side**, not just "fixing" her. --- ### **Why She Might Not See It as Overreacting** - **Emotional Wounds:** If she’s sensitive about cooking (e.g., past criticism, family expectations), even well-meaning feedback can feel like an attack. - **Resentment:** If she feels like she’s **always** the one cooking (even if it’s not great), your critiques may feel like **adding insult to injury**. - **Independence:** Some people **hate being "fixed"**—even if they know they could improve, they may just want to **do things their way**. --- ### **Final Verdict** You **didn’t mean to hurt her**, but your approach **crossed a line** in terms of **how you delivered feedback** and **how you framed her cooking in front of others**. The fact that she’s **withholding a labor of love** (cooking) is a **big red flag**—it’s not just about food, but about **how she feels valued in the relationship**. **AITA?** **Yes, in this context.** But the good news is, **this can be fixed**—if you’re willing to **listen, apologize sincerely, and adjust your behavior**.
